name: Omar Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. This is confidential. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, a chartered accountant with a master’s degree, and I lead reviews of accounts and tax returns at a firm. I handle the difficult clients, check the team’s numbers and use an approved AI helper every day for sorting questions. I like explaining a strange figure to a client more than fixing a spreadsheet in silence. Last-minute requests to rush the team’s checks wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your life like away from that desk?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone, earn about the usual pay for this work and have around three months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby, though not enough to take leaving lightly. I favour a stronger staff voice and public help when jobs change, and I am usually first to try new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team to use the small time savings to call clients about missing records. A faster first draft is fine, but the client still deserves a checked return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am on ordinary accountant pay and have roughly three months of expenses saved, so my own hours feel secure here. I do worry that even modest automation becomes an excuse to overload the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep using the approved AI helper I already use every day to sort receipt questions, and log each correction. I would continue reviewing accounts and tax returns in the first year, and bring the logged errors to our monthly team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about my wages in this version. I feel annoyed at the thought of a colleague getting twice the files with no extra help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is one error you logged this week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The helper treated a client’s personal travel as a business expense, and I caught it against the bank note. I showed the junior reviewer the original note rather than just fixing the total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for more staff now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the partner to keep the junior vacancy open if the queue grows, and show the file count. I would not claim a small time saving proves the whole team can shrink.

say: I would put small **time savings** into calls about clients’ missing records.
I would insist every **tax return** gets checked before a client signs.
think: My **three-month cushion** and ordinary pay make my own hours feel secure here.
I worry a small efficiency will become **extra files** for junior staff.
do: Keep using my **approved AI helper** and log corrections against original records.
Continue reviewing **accounts and returns** and show error logs at monthly team meetings.
feel: I feel **calm** about my income but annoyed by possible extra pressure on juniors.
S0.quote: A faster first draft is fine, but the client still deserves a checked return.
fieldNote: He already uses an **AI helper daily**, but measures it against bank notes and teaches juniors how he found a mistake.
His **staffing concern** is tied to file counts and an open junior vacancy, rather than a claim that all automation harms workers.

steps.text: Continue reviewing client accounts and tax returns each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the firm must share the time saved, not quietly erase junior posts. We should keep a record of which tax notes and checks software takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own review hours could shrink as writing and checking move into software, even if I am one of the stronger accountants. Three months saved and some nearby firms give me room to act, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the staff association to collect hours and vacancy figures from our team, and volunteer to test the approved tax drafting system on five files. In the first year I would use the results to seek a paid client dispute assignment at this firm; if no opening appears, I would look at advertised posts at nearby firms while keeping my current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my role becoming a quality stamp on a machine’s work. The figures and a few alternatives keep me from freezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the association report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count unfilled junior seats, overtime hours and corrected tax drafts, without client names. The partner should see whether the apparent saving is being paid for by people staying late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a dispute assignment worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would need normal pay and protected hours to learn the work, not a new title added to my current pile. I would ask for those terms in writing.

say: I would ask the firm to **share savings** instead of quietly removing junior posts.
I would track which **tax notes** and checks software absorbs.
think: My **review hours** could shrink even though I lead difficult accounts.
A **three-month cushion** and some nearby firms give me limited room to move.
do: Gather **vacancy and overtime** figures through the staff association.
Test **five tax drafts** against source records using the approved system.
Seek an **internal dispute role** only with written normal pay and protected learning hours; otherwise apply to advertised nearby posts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shrinking review hours, but the data gives me a way to act.
S1.quote: The partner should see whether the apparent saving is being paid for by people staying late.
fieldNote: His **progressive outlook** appears in a concrete staff association request for hours and vacancy data, with client names excluded.
He wants **written pay** and protected hours for dispute work; he will keep his job while checking nearby vacancies.

steps.text: Collect junior vacancy and overtime counts through staff association
Test approved tax drafts on five client files
Seek internal dispute role with written normal pay, protected hours; else apply to advertised local posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 hits our accounts and tax work in 2028, not when capable robots turn up around 2031. The staff should see the firm’s staffing plan before cuts land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect cheaper AGI to remove most screen work at our firm, including much of my own review job. I have three months saved, but losing typical accountant pay would use it quickly and nearby vacancies could vanish together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would call a staff association meeting and ask partners for a written hours forecast and a funded route into tax hearings. If they approve fees and paid time in writing, I would enroll in the short hearings course before 2028; in the first year after AGI arrives I would apply for a paid hearings opening if one exists, while keeping any remaining accounts hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the speed, especially for the juniors whose first jobs might disappear. My own buffer buys a little time, not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who gets notice of reduced hours and whether the firm will pay for learning time. We could take a shared set of questions to the partners rather than each person begging alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no hearings opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the three months to search nearby advertised accounting posts, but I would not leave paid accounts work first. I would also ask the association to press for advance notice of any cuts.

say: I would tell colleagues **AGI by 2028** reaches tax desks before capable robots arrive.
I would demand a **written staffing plan** before hours are cut.
think: I expect cheaper AGI to remove most of my **review job** by 2028.
My **three-month buffer** would disappear quickly without ordinary accountant pay.
do: Call a **staff association meeting** and seek a written hours forecast.
Enroll in **tax hearings training** only with written approval of fees and paid time.
Apply for a **paid hearings vacancy** after 2028, keeping accounts hours during any search.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely income loss and the short deadline.
S2.quote: My own buffer buys a little time, not a replacement wage.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** does not protect a desk worker whose accounts and tax reviews are mainly thinking tasks.
He pairs **collective pressure** with a funded personal training route, and keeps current paid hours until a real vacancy appears.

steps.text: Call staff association meeting to seek written hours forecast
Enroll in tax hearings course if fees and paid time receive written approval
Apply for paid hearings vacancy after 2028 while keeping accounts hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to negotiate decent notice and build skills, if the firm starts now. Robots arriving around 2034 do not move the 2031 deadline for tax desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build more savings and get experience with clients before the software changes the core job. Still, a highly skilled accountant is not immune when the skill itself becomes cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the association to propose six months of notice for lost hours, and request firm-paid training in tax hearings with paid time away from returns. If approved in writing, I would enroll next year and save 100 a month while my hours hold; in the first year after 2031 I would move into a paid hearings vacancy if one exists, or keep client reviews while searching advertised posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though five years lets me see whether this path pays. I would not count a hearing role until there is a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the 100 a month come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the second gym membership and pack lunch three days a week. If our hours fall before 2031, that saving target goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for six months of notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives someone on a three-month cushion time to find a new wage before the rent drains it. I would bring that number to our staff association, not just complain in the corridor.

say: I would press for **six months’ notice** of lost hours.
I would remind the firm our **tax deadline** is 2031, before robots arrive.
think: I can build savings, but **accounting skill** could still become cheap.
A paid **hearing role** is only real when there is a contract.
do: Propose **six months’ notice** through the staff association.
Enroll in **tax hearings training** next year with written approval of fees and paid time.
Save **100 monthly** if hours hold; take a contracted paid vacancy after 2031 or keep reviewing while searching.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with more time to test a new line of work.
S3.quote: I would not count a hearing role until there is a contract.
fieldNote: He uses the **five-year runway** to bargain for notice and to test whether client hearings offer paid work.
His **100 monthly** target is explicitly conditional on full hours, and the training requires written approval of fees and paid time.

steps.text: Propose six months of lost-hours notice through staff association
Enroll in hearings course with written fees and paid-time approval
Take contracted paid hearings vacancy after 2031 or search advertised posts while employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 means we have time to agree who benefits from faster accounting. The firm should put junior training and paid client work in the plan, not just software licenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could have a deeper client practice and perhaps a year of expenses saved, if pay holds. Yet most of my written analysis could still be automated when AGI arrives; the 2039 robot date is a separate matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep reviewing accounts and ask my manager to let me lead one complex client meeting each month. If approved, I would keep a record of what clients pay for advice. I would raise my savings transfer to 150 a month if my hours and typical pay hold; in the first year after 2036 I would take a paid advisory vacancy at this firm if the salary and hours are written down, or apply to a nearby advertised firm while keeping my current job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about where this ends, but I do not feel trapped for the next few years. Ten years lets me ask for a fair share and build something clients actually buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for an advisory course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only from savings above six months of expenses, not from rent money. I would first ask whether the firm has a paid course and real client demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a junior colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a junior colleague to learn the tools but also insist on a human reviewer and paid learning hours. An entry job should not become unpaid error checking.

say: I would put **junior training** and paid client work into the firm’s 2036 plan.
I would ask who gets the **time savings** from faster accounting.
think: I could build a **client practice** and larger savings if pay holds.
My written analysis remains **exposed in 2036**, despite the later robot date.
do: Keep **reviewing accounts** and ask my manager to let me lead monthly client meetings; record paid demand if approved.
Save **150 monthly** if current hours and pay hold.
Take a **paid advisory vacancy** after 2036 with written salary and hours, or apply nearby while employed.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about 2036, but secure enough for the next few years.
S4.quote: An entry job should not become unpaid error checking.
fieldNote: His **long-run plan** tests what clients will actually pay for, rather than assuming an advisory title guarantees income.
The **savings transfer** and later move both carry conditions: stable pay now and a written salary and hours for any vacancy.

steps.text: Keep reviewing accounts and ask manager to approve monthly client meetings
Save 150 monthly if hours and typical pay hold
Take paid advisory vacancy with written salary and hours or apply nearby while employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the accounts work could shrink before the firm or staff have a fair plan. Written notice of hours cuts, paid hearings training and a real vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who gets to keep the time the software saves. A junior accountant cannot build judgment if every first job is stripped down to checking the machine.

headlineQuote: A junior accountant cannot build judgment if every first job is stripped down to checking the machine.
portrait: At **27**, Omar leads complex accounts and tax reviews with a master’s degree and chartered accountancy qualification.
He has **typical pay**, three months saved and some nearby job options, while using approved AI tools every day.
His **progressive views** show in staff association demands for notice, paid training and fair use of saved hours.
The **2028 deadline** alarms him; with longer runways, he tests paid client work and builds conditional savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink accounts work before staff have notice, training or a fair staffing plan.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, paid hearings training and an actual vacancy before moving roles.
